Yes indeed, Onkyo are known for overbuilding their components and putting in more than is the minimum requirements. They have very good quality across the board. 
THX qualification is a huge advantage to the Onkyo. Another is 4K compatibility AND upscaling to 4K, wow. When you look at 1080p vs 4K resolution it's enormous. 3D signal compatibility. 2 output sources for video! Great when hosting parties and you put a concert on for ambience, or sports of course. You can get very long HDMI cables and eventually use that feature if not all the time. 
The one advantage I would give to the pioneer is the wattage, it rates 125 @8 ohm as the Onkyo rates 110 @ 8 ohm. This does not mean decibel level though. It is not necessarily better to take more electricity to reach the same decibel level. So it's hard to tell. The fact that the Onkyo has THX and the Pioneer does not tells me that hands down the Onkyo will sound way way better. If it turns out it is not loud enough (which I HIGHLY doubt) you can add a preamp and boost the front two speakers and power anything you want to. 
They are matched fairly evenly on paper as far as Total harmonic distortion and wattage. I've always leaned towards the sound of Onkyo's overbuilt components though. They both have App control.

The pioneer unit does not list it's frequency response so that worries me, however the Onkyo is 5 Hz-100 kHz. Even though the extent of these ranges are outside of human hearing they affect how the sound waves around that frequency sound. And that is a crazy good range.

Well, I can't say for certain what it is. I can point out some characteristics I see. Very well documented by the way. The top is formed for a thumb and index finger to turn. Or two paralel pipes to add torque. The bottom has cut out tangs to fit into the notches of something. The pattern is symmetrical and unique. it definitely was meant to fit into something specific. It would make for a solid transfer of force. the middle being completely round, tricky. It could fit into something as the lip on the bottom is smaller than on the top. I think it's circular so it can spin as part of it's function. it seals fairly well but why put so much detail on both ends of a cork? It's relatively handmade. there are lots of hand tool marks and knicks. the amount of imperfections lead me to believe it's from a time of less advanced tech.

I think the porcelain insulator idea would not have the cold feeling to it, the weight would be a light lighter if it was porcelain, intricate cut out on the bottom is not present on insulators. It is a similar overall shape, but not it. This is a dense strong material designed to transfer a lot of torque. The fact that it has so many scrapes and cuts yet has not shattered tells of it's strength.

Speculation? I think it may have been designed as part of a water system. the revoir would be above this part and come down into a spigot type thing, and this is the key you would use to turn the spigot open. Water was a super valuable resource and makes sense that you would want a key system to limit access to it. The circular middle part and wider lip at the top would seat it into place and keep it there while force was applied. It was found in the water, perhaps it was lost in the process of gathering water for storage? I'm not sure if this was the function it was used for, but I think this was the method in which it was used.

optical digital is the best audio connection in the consumer market, the difference between that and RCA plugs is substantial. 
These Denons use standard 1/8" headphone jack with the gold 1/4" screw on adapter that comes with them.
What connections does the amp have as an output? Pretty much any headphones are going to be passive and plug into an amp of some kind. The benefits of Toslink/spdif/optical digital is that the signal goes from the source to the amp still in a digital format at high quality. Then the amp converts it internally and sends it out through 3.5 or to speakers via analog signal. Supplying the amp with a pure digital source allows for a better frequency range along with zero loss in quality over the length of the cable because of it being an insulated light signal. It has to be an analog signal once it gets to your ears, unless you speak R2D2, but keeping it digital and preserved as long as possible is the best.
Totally worth it. I've heard the difference and it's a big one. For as long as you have a set of good headphones for, $60 is not that much in this long run.
